content: Oxacillin is an antibiotic approved by the FDA for treating infections caused by penicillinase-producing Staphylococci. Common side effects include rash, diarrhea, and nausea. Adult Indications and Dosage Oxacillin is indicated for infections caused by penicillinase-producing Staphylococci that are susceptible to the drug. Initial cultures and susceptibility tests should be performed to identify the causative organism and its sensitivity to oxacillin. Oxacillin can be used empirically in suspected resistant staphylococcal infections before susceptibility results are available. It should not be used for infections caused by organisms susceptible to penicillin G. If susceptibility tests reveal the infection is due to an organism other than resistant Staphylococcus, oxacillin therapy should be discontinued. To prevent the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain the effectiveness of oxacillin, it should only be used for infections proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. Local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns may guide empiric therapy in the absence of specific data. Off-Label Use and Dosage (Adult) Limited information is available regarding off-label guideline-supported use of oxacillin in adults. Non-guideline-supported uses include: Bacteremia associated with intravascular lines caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). Bacterial meningitis caused by MSSA. Bone infections and infectious disease prophylaxis related to catheter complications. Pediatric Indications and Dosage Limited information is available regarding FDA-labeled use of oxacillin in pediatric patients. Off-label guideline-supported and non-guideline-supported uses in pediatric patients are also limited. Contraindications Oxacillin is contraindicated in patients with a history of hypersensitivity (anaphylactic) reactions to any penicillin. Solutions containing dextrose may be contraindicated in patients with known allergies to corn or corn products. Warnings Serious and sometimes fatal hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylactic shock, have occurred in patients receiving penicillin. These reactions are more common with parenteral administration but can also occur with oral penicillins. Penicillin therapy should only be initiated after a thorough drug and allergy history is obtained. Cross-reactivity may occur in individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity when treated with cephalosporins. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including oxacillin. CDAD can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile may require colectomy in severe cases. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even up to two months after administration. Adverse Reactions Allergic reactions to penicillins can be immediate or delayed. Immediate reactions occur within 20 minutes and range from urticaria to anaphylaxis. Delayed reactions may occur after 48 hours and include fever, rash, and other systemic symptoms. Gastrointestinal irritation, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and stomatitis, may occur, especially with oral therapy. Neurotoxic reactions, such as seizures, may occur with high intravenous doses, particularly in patients with renal insufficiency. Renal tubular damage and interstitial nephritis have been reported infrequently, presenting with rash, fever, eosinophilia, and renal insufficiency. Pseudomembranous colitis and hepatotoxicity, characterized by elevated liver enzymes, have been associated with oxacillin use. Drug Interactions Tetracycline, a bacteriostatic antibiotic, may antagonize the bactericidal effect of penicillin, and concurrent use should be avoided. Probenecid may prolong oxacillin blood levels by inhibiting renal tubular secretion of penicillins. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Oxacillin is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA. Animal studies have not shown evidence of harm to the fetus, but adequate human studies are lacking. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Nursing Mothers: Penicillins are excreted in human milk. Caution is advised when administering to nursing women. Pediatric Use: Due to immature renal function in pediatric patients, oxacillin may not be completely excreted, leading to elevated blood levels. Frequent monitoring and dosage adjustments are recommended. Geriatric Use: Elderly patients may have reduced renal, hepatic, or cardiac function, necessitating cautious dose selection and monitoring of renal function. Oxacillin is substantially excreted by the kidneys, and the risk of toxic reactions may be higher in patients with impaired renal function. Administration and Monitoring Oxacillin can be administered orally or intravenously. Renal function should be monitored in elderly patients, and dosage adjustments may be necessary to avoid neurotoxic reactions. Liver function tests (AST and ALT) should be periodically obtained during therapy to monitor for abnormalities. Pediatric patients should be closely monitored for clinical and laboratory evidence of toxicity or adverse effects. Overdosage Signs and symptoms of oxacillin overdose are consistent with those described in the adverse reactions section. Discontinue the medication, treat symptomatically, and provide supportive care as needed. Pharmacology Oxacillin is a penicillinase-resistant penicillin that exerts bactericidal action by inhibiting bacterial cell wall biosynthesis during active multiplication. Storage Oxacillin injection should be stored at or below -20°C (-4°F). Patient Counseling Patients should be informed about the potential for allergic reactions and advised to report any symptoms immediately. They should also be counseled on the importance of completing the full course of therapy to prevent resistance. Alcohol Interaction The interaction between alcohol and oxacillin has not been established. Patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol consumption while on this medication.
